verdicts.note: Page: 'written in a fluent, seemingly translucent style that may distract the reader from realizing that it can only be understood when every word is adhered to literally'. Quote verbatim; both limbs supported. Clute says this of 'The Fifth Head of Cerberus' as his worked example of the essay's general law that 'every word he wrote was meant'.

Page: 'like so many other houses in Wolfe's work, where the home of the narrator is likely to combine the features of a prison, a "pleasure garden," and a tomb'. The assigned quote 'the home of the narrator of a typical Wolfe tale' appears verbatim in the very next clause (the skull-analogue sentence).

Page: 'It is also very likely that the home of a Wolfe narrator will also serve as a laboratory, whose subject is that narrator.' Quote verbatim; 'experimental subject' is carried by the surrounding Skinner-Box passage and 'He is an experiment.'

Page quotes the tale's opening line, then: 'informing us immediately that (as with so much of Wolfe) we are reading a memoir, one that ... we are meant to understand has actually been written down'. Quote verbatim; first-sentence, at-once, memoir and physically-written-down limbs all supported.

Page: 'academics have notoriously tended to shun him for decades: because you cannot strip-mine Gene Wolfe for "meaning," you cannot abstract themes from stories that only make sense when it is understood how they have been told.' Quote verbatim. Clute hedges the causal link ('which may be one of the reasons') and names a second reason ('he is indeed difficult'); the claim states the reason more firmly than the page but does not misname it.
Page: 'Ironically, Severian is unreliable because of the very characteristic that makes him appear wholly reliable: his eidetic memory.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

Page: 'Even the concealment of the story driving the plot of The Book of the New Sun is explicable in terms of Severian's characterisation, given that mnemonists have a tendency to remember a wealth of detail (plot) which scatters meaning (story).' Quote verbatim; concealment, wealth-of-detail and scattered-meaning limbs all supported.

Page: 'The gulf between plot and story, between the apparent and the real, alerts the reader to the fact that Wolfe is playing a complex and contrived textual game.' Quote verbatim; 'signal that alerts the reader to Wolfe's game' is the page's own wording.

Page: 'Reconciling plot with story, perceiving the text not as the religious document it purports to be but as the product of a manipulated individual caught in the Hierogrammates' evolutionary machinations ... is the first step towards understanding Wolfe's strategies and purpose.' Quote verbatim; 'first task' = 'first step', 'manipulated narrator' = the manipulated individual (Severian).

verdicts.trueWording: little to distinguish it apart from its polished, literate style
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'little in the prose surface ... to distinguish it' — the page names 'the polished, literate style' (with xenography and credible characters) as an explicit EXCEPTION to what is undistinguished, so the prose surface is the one thing Wright says does stand out
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim: 'On a first, superficial reading, there is little to distinguish Wolfe's tetralogy from many other sf and fantasy novels, with the exception of the aforementioned xenography, or world building, the credible characters and the polished, literate style. The plot itself is apparently unremarkable.' Wright's undistinguished element is the PLOT, not the prose; the claim inverts the exception clause.

Page: 'critics like Michael Bishop were lauding The Shadow of the Torturer for being: an immediately accessible book for anyone with moderate intelligence and the ability to read.' Quote verbatim (page continues 'and the ability to read'); footnote 2 sources it to Bishop, Thrust, Fall 1980.

verdicts.trueWording: Budrys, a reviewer inside the guild of writers, sees the moves' concealment
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'a working novelist' — the page never calls Budrys a novelist (the word 'novelist' does not occur anywhere on the page); Wright identifies him only as a reviewer (footnote 3: review of The Claw of the Conciliator, F&SF, June 1980), and the only status cue is Budrys's own bracketed gloss 'those outside the guild [of writers]'
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'I am in the presence of a practitioner whose moves I cannot follow; I see only the same illusions that are seen by those outside the guild [of writers]. I know the cards are up the sleeves somewhere, but there are clearly extra arms to this person.' The cards-up-the-sleeve and cannot-follow-the-moves limbs are fully supported; only the 'working novelist' descriptor is not on the page.

Page: 'Although Searles prophesied that The Book of the New Sun was "certainly the sort of novel that will provide a field day for critics, essayists, people who make lists, analysers, and academics", his prophecy has gone largely unfulfilled, with the notable exception of Michael Andre-Driussi's commendable Lexicon Urthus (1994).' Quote verbatim; 'twenty years on' is supported by the preceding paragraph, 'Twenty years after the publication of The Shadow of the Torturer'.

Page quotes Searles: 'It will undoubtedly be considered a landmark in the field, one that perhaps marks the turning point of science fiction from content to style, from matter to manner.' Quote verbatim; 'possible' = 'perhaps'; footnote 5 sources it to Searles's review of The Citadel of the Autarch, IASFM, May 1983.

Page (Person's question sets up 'characters all speaking in turn, without being identified'), Wolfe: 'When Maytera Marble talks, she is saying something that only Maytera Marble would say. When Blood speaks, he is saying something that only Blood would say. And so the reader, if the reader is intelligent, knows who said that from what was said.' Quote verbatim; page header confirms Lawrence Person, Nova Express Vol. 5 No. 1, Fall/Winter 1998.
